result.summary: Pausanias reflects on the ruin of Megalopolis and lists other once-great cities that fell, and new ones that rose. He ends with islands that sank or appeared, concluding that human affairs are unstable.

scenes.title: Cities Rise and Fall
scenes.summary: Pausanias argues that fortune and the deity overturn cities, citing Mycenae, Nineveh, Thebes, Babylon, Delos and others against newly risen Alexandria and Seleucia.

scenes.title: Islands Sunk and Born
scenes.summary: Pausanias gives the examples of Chryse, swallowed by the sea near Lemnos, and the new island Hiera, and closes on the instability of human affairs.

characters.name: Philoctetes
characters.description: hero said to have been bitten by a watersnake on Chryse

notable_quotes.reason: Concise statement of the passage's moral about the instability of human affairs.

analysis.text: The section treats fortune and the deity as forces that constantly reverse the standing of cities, explaining Megalopolis's decline as part of a general pattern.
Pausanias writes under the Roman Empire, when old Greek centres were depopulated while Hellenistic foundations like Alexandria and Seleucia flourished.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias says Delos had no population apart from Athenians sent to guard the temple, reflecting its decline after the sack of 88 and 69 BC.

language_notes.text: "I nothing marvel at" is archaic word order meaning "I am not at all surprised."
"With a high hand" means arbitrarily and overbearingly, with absolute power.
"Emporium" means a great trading centre or marketplace.
Bel is the Babylonian god Marduk's title, "Lord"; his temple is the great ziggurat sanctuary of Babylon.
Philoctetes was bitten by a snake on the way to Troy; the wound festered and the Greeks left him on an island.

context_notes.text: Mycenae was Agamemnon's city, leader of the Greek expedition against Troy (Ilium); it was destroyed by Argos in the fifth century BC.
Delos was Apollo's sacred island; Athens administered it and sent officials to guard the temple.
Alexandria was founded by Alexander the Great and Seleucia by Seleucus I, both in the late fourth century BC, so they were relatively new.

literary_notes.text: Fortune is treated as a ruler who "reduces everything in subjection," making chance seem an active, domineering power.
The new, flourishing cities are set against the ruined ancient ones, driving home the argument about fortune's reversals.
The exclamatory closing remark sums up the moral of the chapter in a brief, emotional aphorism.
